chunks.text:
ADT and Data Structure
- ADT: the data and its operations
- Says what, not how
- Data structure: an implementation in a language

An abstract data type (ADT) is a description of a kind of data and the operations allowed on it, for example add, remove, and contains. An ADT says what the operations do. It does not say how the data is kept in memory, and it does not depend on a programming language.

A data structure is a concrete way to store data in a program, written in a specific language. It implements the operations of an ADT. The same ADT can have several data structures behind it, such as an array-based version and a linked version.

cases.script: An abstract data type describes the data and the operations allowed on it, but not how the data is kept in memory. A data structure is the concrete version written in a specific language that implements those operations.
cases.note: Rewording. (Stage 12 prep experiment, labeled by the user 2026-11-06)

chunks.text:
Collections
- Bag
- Set
- List
- Stack
- Queue
- Map
A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.

A stack adds and removes items at the same end, so the last item added is the first removed (LIFO). A queue adds items at the back and removes them from the front, so the first item added is the first removed (FIFO). A map stores pairs of a key and a value and finds a value by its key.

cases.script: Here are six collections. A bag and a set keep no order, but only a bag allows duplicates. A list keeps a sequence with positions, a stack removes the last item added, a queue removes the first item added, and a map finds a value by its key.
cases.note: Rewording of the two reference chunks. (Stage 12 prep experiment, labeled by the user 2026-11-06)

chunks.text:
Encapsulation
- Keep data and methods together
- Hide the data inside the class
- Use it through public methods

Encapsulation puts an object's data and the methods that use that data together in one class, and keeps the data from being changed directly from outside. In Java the fields are usually declared private, and other code works with the object through public methods.

cases.script: Encapsulation keeps an object's data and its methods together and hides the data inside the class; other code uses public methods. It is like a TV remote: you press the buttons without opening the case.
cases.note: Own comparison tied to the hiding idea; no new fact. (Stage 12 prep experiment, labeled by the user 2026-11-06)
